beginner_glossary.Burn-in (test): Stress-testing chips at high temperature and voltage to make the weak ones fail in the factory rather than in the field. It screens out 'infant mortality' defects, so only reliable chips ship. Aehr makes the equipment that does this. The more expensive and mission-critical the chip (AI processors, power devices, photonics), the more valuable burn-in becomes.
beginner_glossary.Wafer-Level Burn-In (WLBI) / FOX platfor: Testing/burning-in ALL the chips on a whole silicon wafer AT ONCE, before they are cut apart and packaged — saving cost on high-value devices. Aehr's 'FOX' systems (FOX-XP, FOX-NP) plus its 'WaferPak' full-wafer contactors do this. Aehr says FOX-XP is the only production-proven full-wafer test+burn-in for high-power devices (silicon carbide, photonics, AI processors).
beginner_glossary.Package-Level Burn-In (PLBI) / Sonoma pl: Burning-in chips AFTER they're packaged — the current industry standard for many parts. Aehr's 'Sonoma' (and Tahoe/Echo) systems, gained via the Incal Technology acquisition, do ultra-high-power package-level burn-in — important for power-hungry AI processors.
beginner_glossary.WaferPak: Aehr's full-wafer contactor — the consumable interface that connects the test system to every chip on a wafer. These are a recurring, higher-margin 'consumable' revenue stream alongside the systems.
beginner_glossary.Book-to-bill ratio: Bookings (new orders) divided by billings (revenue) in a period. Above 1.0 means orders are coming in faster than revenue is recognized — a sign of future growth. Aehr's was OVER 3.5x in Q3 FY2026 (orders far exceeded revenue), the core bull signal.
beginner_glossary.Bookings: The dollar value of new orders received. Aehr booked $37.2M in Q3 FY2026 — far above the $10.3M of revenue that quarter — pointing to a future revenue ramp IF those orders convert.
beginner_glossary.Silicon carbide (SiC) power semiconducto: A type of high-efficiency power chip used heavily in electric vehicles. SiC was Aehr's historical core market; the EV slowdown caused a downturn that cut Aehr's revenue from FY2024–FY2026.
beginner_glossary.AI processor / custom AI ASIC: The chips that run AI — either GPUs or custom 'ASICs' designed by hyperscalers (e.g., Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium). They are large, expensive, and must be reliable, which is driving new demand for Aehr's burn-in.
beginner_glossary.HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory): Stacked memory placed next to an AI processor. Burning-in AI processors WITH HBM at high power is a new, demanding application Aehr is targeting (HTOL modules).
beginner_glossary.HTOL (High-Temperature Operating Life): A reliability/qualification test that runs chips hot for a long time to prove they'll last. Aehr is developing HTOL burn-in modules for high-power AI processors.
beginner_glossary.Silicon photonics / optical I/O: Chips that move data with light instead of electricity — used for fast data-center optical interconnects in AI clusters. Aehr won silicon-photonics customers for wafer-level burn-in of these optical ICs, a new growth vector tied to AI networking.
beginner_glossary.Hyperscaler: A giant cloud/AI company (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta). Aehr's 'lead hyperscale customer' is buying its burn-in systems for custom AI ASIC processors.
beginner_glossary.Total Addressable Market (TAM): The total potential sales opportunity. Aehr argues its TAM is expanding as it moves from SiC into AI processors, photonics, and memory — each a large new burn-in opportunity.
beginner_glossary.GAAP vs Non-GAAP: GAAP = official accounting results. Non-GAAP strips out items like stock-based compensation and one-offs. Aehr's GAAP and non-GAAP can differ (e.g., FY2025 GAAP was a small loss while non-GAAP was a small profit).
beginner_glossary.Price-to-sales (P/S): Market value divided by revenue. Because Aehr is small and currently unprofitable, P/E doesn't work; investors look at P/S — and Aehr's is very high (~75x trailing), reflecting big growth expectations baked into the stock.

company_snapshot.what_it_is: Aehr Test Systems is a small-cap maker of semiconductor TEST and BURN-IN equipment. Its machines stress-test chips (at high temperature/voltage) to weed out unreliable ones before they ship. In the AI/semiconductor supply chain it would sit in the EQUIPMENT tier (a reliability/burn-in tool vendor). Historically its core market was silicon-carbide (SiC) power chips for electric vehicles; that market is in a downturn, and Aehr is pivoting hard toward burn-in for AI PROCESSORS (custom ASICs with HBM), SILICON PHOTONICS (optical I/O for data-center interconnects), and memory — all tied to the AI data-center build-out.
company_snapshot.founder_ceo: President & CEO: Gayn Erickson. Founded 1977.
company_snapshot.manufacturing_footprint: Designs and builds its FOX (wafer-level) and Sonoma (package-level) burn-in systems and WaferPak/consumables; U.S.-based operations (Fremont, CA). The Sonoma package-level burn-in line came via the acquisition of Incal Technology.
end_markets: AI processors / custom AI ASICs (with HBM)
Silicon carbide (SiC) power semiconductors (EV — legacy core, in downturn)
Flash memory, gallium nitride (GaN), and other high-value devices

business_model.summary: Aehr sells capital equipment (burn-in/test SYSTEMS) plus recurring CONSUMABLES (WaferPak full-wafer contactors and related parts). A customer buys a FOX (wafer-level) or Sonoma (package-level) system, then keeps buying the consumables and additional capacity as production scales. The business is lumpy and customer-concentrated: a few large orders can swing a quarter. The thesis is a market shift — from a SiC/EV downturn that has been shrinking revenue, toward a much larger AI/data-center burn-in opportunity (AI processors, photonics, memory) where Aehr's high-power, wafer-level capability is differentiated. The leading indicator is BOOKINGS, which have inflected sharply even while reported revenue is still depressed.
how_they_make_money: Burn-in/test SYSTEMS: FOX wafer-level (WLBI) and Sonoma package-level (PLBI) systems sold to chipmakers, test houses, and hyperscalers. [company releases 2026]
CONSUMABLES & contactors: WaferPak full-wafer contactors and related recurring parts that scale with customers' production volumes — a stickier, higher-margin stream. [company releases]
Service/support and capacity add-ons: follow-on orders as customers expand burn-in capacity (a recurring pattern with the lead hyperscale and photonics customers). [company releases 2026]
competitive_moat_analyst_view: Differentiated high-power, wafer-level burn-in: Aehr positions FOX-XP as the only production-proven FULL-WAFER test+burn-in for high-power devices (SiC, photonics, AI processors) — a hard, specialized capability. [company releases]
Dual-platform reach: wafer-level (FOX) PLUS package-level (Sonoma) lets Aehr serve both pre- and post-package burn-in, widening its addressable market. [company releases]

Early AI-burn-in positioning + reference wins: initial Sonoma order from a lead hyperscaler's next-gen AI ASIC, a paid 300mm wafer-level evaluation with a top-tier AI processor supplier, and new silicon-photonics customers — reference accounts in fast-growing markets. [company releases 2026]
Consumables lock-in: once a customer standardizes on Aehr's WaferPak/system, ongoing consumable and capacity purchases follow.

ASSUMPTION-flavored: these are real edges, but Aehr is SMALL, customer-concentrated, and the AI-burn-in opportunity is still mostly in BOOKINGS/evaluations rather than proven, recurring high-volume revenue.

revenue_streams.analyst_view: Aehr's income statement and its order book are telling OPPOSITE stories right now: revenue is DOWN (SiC/EV trough — $10.3M in Q3) while BOOKINGS are inflecting UP (>$37M, book-to-bill 3.5x) on AI processors and silicon photonics. That divergence is the entire investment debate. The bulls focus on the bookings/TAM-expansion (AI burn-in as a multi-year driver replacing SiC); the bears note that revenue is still small and declining, the company is unprofitable, and the wins are early (evaluations, initial orders) rather than proven high-volume production. Until bookings convert into sustained revenue, the reported financials will look weak relative to the stock's expectations.

competitors.landscape_summary: Aehr is a niche specialist in wafer-level and high-power burn-in. It competes with larger, broader semiconductor test & burn-in equipment makers and with chipmakers' in-house/alternative test approaches. Its edge is specialized high-power, full-wafer burn-in; its disadvantage is small size and customer concentration versus much bigger test-equipment peers.

key_competitors.note: Japanese test-equipment giant (ATE/SoC test, incl. burn-in adjacencies) — far larger; a key AI-test beneficiary.
Major automated-test-equipment (ATE) maker; broad semiconductor test exposure including AI/HPC.
Test handling, interface, and inspection; competes/overlaps in back-end test and burn-in-adjacent equipment.
Large chipmakers and test houses may use internal or alternative burn-in methods rather than buying Aehr systems.
Specialty suppliers compete on the consumable (contactor/WaferPak-equivalent) layer.

competitors.differentiation_analyst_view: Aehr's differentiation is being a focused leader in HIGH-POWER, WAFER-LEVEL burn-in — a hard, specialized niche that matters for SiC, photonics, and high-power AI processors — plus a package-level option (Sonoma) for the standard flow. The risks are that (1) it is tiny relative to Advantest/Teradyne, (2) revenue is concentrated in a few large customers/orders, and (3) bigger players or customers' in-house solutions could encroach as AI burn-in becomes a larger prize. The competitive question is whether Aehr's early reference wins translate into a durable, scaling franchise before larger rivals fully target the same applications.

financial_performance.analyst_view: Aehr's financials show a company at a TROUGH in revenue (SiC/EV downturn) and currently unprofitable, but with a sharply inflecting ORDER book pointed at AI/data-center burn-in. FY2025 revenue was $59.0M (small GAAP loss), TTM revenue has fallen to ~$45M with an ~$11M net loss, yet Q3 FY2026 bookings of $37.2M (book-to-bill 3.5x) and H2 bookings guided to $60–80M imply a coming revenue ramp. The crux: this is a 'bookings-ahead-of-revenue' inflection story — credible given the named hyperscaler/photonics wins, but unproven until those orders show up as sustained, profitable revenue.

It should be judged on bookings conversion, TAM capture, and the path to profitability — not on today's revenue or earnings.

valuation.analyst_view: This is the report's most important honest flag: AEHR trades at ~$108 while the (sparse, April-dated) analyst targets cluster around $56–$68 — i.e., the stock is ~40% ABOVE consensus, on ~75x DECLINING sales, while unprofitable. That combination says the share price is driven by momentum and AI-burn-in optionality running ahead of both current fundamentals and analyst marks. The bull case (real, named hyperscaler/photonics wins; book-to-bill 3.5x; expanding TAM) is genuine, but the valuation prices in a lot of future success; the bear case is simply that a tiny, unprofitable, revenue-declining company at 75x sales has significant downside if the AI-burn-in ramp disappoints or is slower/lumpier than hoped. High risk, high volatility, binary-feeling on execution.

final_research_summary.one_paragraph: Aehr Test Systems (AEHR) is a small-cap maker of semiconductor BURN-IN and test equipment — machines that stress-test chips to screen out unreliable ones before they ship. (NOTE: it is not yet a node in this project's supply-chain graph; this is a standalone report.) Historically its core market was silicon-carbide (SiC) power chips for EVs; that market is in a downturn, so revenue has been FALLING — FY2025 (ended 2025-05-30) revenue was $59.0M (a small GAAP loss), and TTM revenue is ~$45.3M with an ~$11.4M net loss. The story is a PIVOT to AI: burn-in for AI processors (custom ASICs with HBM), silicon photonics (optical I/O for data-center interconnects), and memory. The evidence of that pivot is in the ORDER BOOK, not yet the income statement: Q3 FY2026 (ended 2026-02-27) revenue was just $10.3M, but BOOKINGS were $37.2M — a book-to-bill of over 3.5x — driven by an initial Sonoma order from a lead hyperscaler's next-gen AI ASIC, a paid 300mm wafer-level burn-in evaluation with a top-tier AI processor supplier, and new silicon-photonics wins; management guided H2 FY2026 bookings to the high end of $60–80M. The valuation is the central caution: at ~$108 the stock is up roughly 10x off its 52-week low ($10.89–$121.80 range) for a ~$3.41B market cap on ~$45M of DECLINING revenue (~75x trailing sales) while UNPROFITABLE — and it trades ~40% ABOVE the (thin, April-dated) analyst targets of ~$56–$68. What is FACT is a genuine, named AI/data-center burn-in bookings inflection (book-to-bill 3.5x) on top of a depressed, currently loss-making base; what is being PRICED is that those bookings convert into a much larger, profitable AI-burn-in franchise. The debate is execution/conversion and an extreme valuation, not whether the AI-burn-in opportunity is real.

beginner_glossary.ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Ci: A chip custom-designed for ONE specific job (e.g., a particular company's AI accelerator), as opposed to a flexible, off-the-shelf chip like an NVIDIA GPU. Alchip helps companies design and manufacture their own ASICs.
beginner_glossary.Custom silicon / XPU: A hyperscaler's own AI accelerator chip (Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium, etc.). Big cloud companies build these to cut cost and reduce dependence on NVIDIA. 'XPU' is a generic term for such custom accelerators. Alchip is one of the firms that turns these designs into real, manufacturable chips.
beginner_glossary.ASIC design service house: A company that provides the engineering to take a chip from concept/architecture to a finished, manufacturable product — physical design, integration, and managing manufacturing/packaging/test. Alchip, Broadcom, Marvell, and GUC are examples. Alchip is a PURE design-service house (it sells no chips or IP of its own).
beginner_glossary.NRE (Non-Recurring Engineering): The one-time design fees a customer pays Alchip to engineer a chip BEFORE any volume production. NRE is high-margin and front-loaded; it was 'very strong' in Q1 2026 and is what kept margins high while production revenue was low.
beginner_glossary.Production revenue (vs NRE): Once a chip is designed, Alchip also earns money making/shipping it in volume (it buys wafers from TSMC, has them packaged/tested, and sells finished chips to the customer). Production revenue is larger but lower-margin than NRE. The 2026 story is production revenue ramping as the N3 accelerator ships.
beginner_glossary.COT (Customer-Owned Tooling): A business model where the customer owns the chip design/IP and hires Alchip mainly to implement and manufacture it. As volumes get huge, hyperscalers increasingly prefer COT — which Alchip says favors a neutral service house like itself.
beginner_glossary.PD0 / PD1 / PD2: Levels of how much design work Alchip does. Higher PD levels (PD1/PD2) mean Alchip adds more design value (higher margin); 'production-only' work adds the least value and lowest margin. Alchip is cautious about taking production-only jobs.
beginner_glossary.Physical design / back-end integration: The engineering that turns a chip's logical design into the actual transistor-level layout that can be manufactured, then stitches all the pieces (compute die, I/O die, memory) into one working chip. This is Alchip's core expertise; it says it is the ONLY physical-design vendor for its N3 and N2 accelerator projects.
beginner_glossary.Process node (N3 / N2 / N5 / N7): TSMC's chip-manufacturing generations ('N3' = 3-nanometer-class, 'N2' = 2nm). Smaller numbers = newer, faster, denser, more expensive. Alchip works at the leading edge: N3/N2/N5/N7 were >80% of its Q1 2026 revenue. The shift from N3 to N2 roughly doubles the value Alchip captures per project.
beginner_glossary.Tape-out: The moment a chip design is finalized and sent to the foundry (TSMC) to be manufactured. Alchip plans to 'tape out' its N2 accelerator by end of 2026, with production revenue ~2028.
beginner_glossary.HPC (High-Performance Computing): Data-center computing for AI and heavy workloads. HPC was 70% of Alchip's Q1 2026 revenue — i.e., AI accelerators are its main business.
beginner_glossary.Chiplet: Instead of one big chip, a design split into several smaller 'tiles' (compute die, I/O die, etc.) packaged together. The N2 accelerator is a chiplet design, which raises both complexity and the price/value Alchip captures.
beginner_glossary.CoWoS / advanced packaging: TSMC's flagship method of combining the processor with stacks of HBM memory into one large AI package. Alchip secures CoWoS capacity for its customers; it says wafers (not CoWoS) are currently the bottleneck.
beginner_glossary.HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory): Stacked DRAM placed next to an AI chip for fast data access. In Alchip's projects the HBM is 'consigned' (supplied by the customer), not bought by Alchip.
beginner_glossary.Wafer / wafer capacity / turnaround time: A wafer is the silicon disk on which chips are made. 'N3 capacity is the most precious thing in the industry' — getting enough leading-edge wafers from TSMC limits how much Alchip can ship. The full turnaround (wafer + CoWoS) is ~6–7 months, which caps near-term upside.
beginner_glossary.Gross margin: Percent of revenue left after the direct cost of the work. Alchip's was a high 50% in Q1 2026 because of the NRE-heavy mix; management expects it to TREND DOWN later in 2026 as lower-margin production revenue grows (even though total profit rises).
beginner_glossary.EPS (Earnings Per Share): Net profit per share. Q1 2026 EPS was NT$17.55; FY2025 was NT$69.2; trailing-twelve-month was NT$67.05 (2026-06-13).
beginner_glossary.P/E ratio / Forward P/E: Share price divided by earnings per share. Alchip's TRAILING P/E was ~61x (on depressed 2025/early-2026 earnings) but FORWARD P/E only ~24x (2026-06-13) — the gap reflects how much earnings are expected to recover as the N3 ramp hits.

company_snapshot.what_it_is: Alchip is a Taiwan-listed (Cayman-incorporated) PURE-PLAY ASIC design-service company. It does NOT sell its own chips or IP; instead it engineers and manufactures CUSTOM silicon for other companies — most importantly, the AI accelerators (custom 'XPUs') that hyperscalers build to rival NVIDIA's GPUs. In the AI/semiconductor supply chain it sits in the chip-design/component layer: it takes a customer's accelerator design, does the physical design and integration on TSMC's leading-edge nodes (N3, N2), secures wafer + CoWoS + substrate + test capacity, and ships finished chips. Its self-described edge is NEUTRALITY — because it makes no competing products, every IP and packaging partner is willing to work with it.

It is deliberately diversifying its ENGINEERING resources outside China (Japan office up to 250 staff; Malaysia + Vietnam 120+ engineers combined) to manage geopolitical risk; China work is focused on automotive/robotics/consumer at N3 and above. business_model.summary: Alchip earns money in two linked phases. First, NRE (non-recurring engineering): high-margin, front-loaded design fees a customer pays to have Alchip engineer a chip. Second, PRODUCTION: once the chip is designed, Alchip buys the wafers from TSMC, manages packaging/test, and sells finished chips in volume — larger revenue but lower margin. The whole company is a leveraged bet on the rise of CUSTOM AI silicon: as hyperscalers build their own accelerators to cut cost and reduce NVIDIA dependence, they need a neutral, leading-edge design-service partner — which is exactly what Alchip is. Revenue is lumpy because it swings between NRE-heavy (design) and production-heavy phases per chip generation.
how_they_make_money: NRE design fees (high margin, front-loaded): engineering custom accelerators, CPUs, and networking ASICs — 'very strong', especially from North American hyperscalers. [Q1 2026 call]

Production / volume chip sales (larger, lower margin): shipping finished chips (e.g., the N3 AI accelerator ramping from June 2026), where Alchip sources TSMC wafers + CoWoS + substrate + test. [Q1 2026 call]
By application (Q1 2026): HPC/AI accelerators 70% of revenue; plus automotive (China), networking ASICs, and selective Arm server CPUs. [Q1 2026 call]
competitive_moat_analyst_view: Neutrality: Alchip sells no chips or IP of its own, so it has no conflict of interest with customers — every IP/packaging/optical partner (e.g., Ayar Labs, NVLink ecosystem) will work with it. Management calls this its core differentiator vs. product-making rivals. [Q1 2026 call]
Leading-edge physical-design expertise: it claims to be the ONLY physical-design vendor on its N3 and N2 accelerator projects, and a leader in number of tape-outs/design wins.
TSMC relationship + capacity access: tight cooperation with TSMC for scarce N3 wafers and CoWoS — a real advantage when wafers are the bottleneck.
Anchor accelerator customer: one dominant hyperscaler accelerator account (see customer concentration risk) that is 'one of the most important accounts in the industry'.

ASSUMPTION-flavored: the moat is real in pure-play ASIC service, but Broadcom and Marvell are far larger and also enable custom silicon; Alchip's edge is being the focused, neutral specialist rather than the biggest.

So the stock is NOT cheap, but it is priced as a recovery/growth story rather than on trough earnings. The key swing factors are (1) the N3 ramp landing on time and at good yield, (2) full-year revenue actually surpassing the 2024 peak, and (3) the N2 generation scaling in 2028.

analyst_targets_facts.note: Targets are dispersed and the stock is volatile — check each source's date. Alchip gives no numeric guidance, so targets vary widely with each analyst's ramp assumptions.
analyst_targets_facts.consensus: Consensus rating 'Buy' — roughly 23 analysts (about 13 buy + 8 strong buy + 2 hold, 0 sell). Average 12-month target ~NT$5,733 (one widely-cited source), implying meaningful upside from ~NT$4,105.
analyst_targets_facts.range: Target range ~NT$3,755 (low) to ~NT$6,542 (high) — a wide spread; some trackers show a lower average (~NT$4,460), so dispersion is high and depends heavily on N3/N2 ramp assumptions.

valuation.analyst_view: This is a high-beta, small-cap (~US$10.5B) leveraged play on custom AI silicon — very different from a megacap. The bull view: forward P/E ~24x is reasonable for a company about to grow revenue past its prior peak with visibility to 2029. The bear view: the multiple still assumes a flawless N3 ramp and continued reliance on essentially ONE dominant accelerator customer, in a small, volatile name where any slip (yield, wafer allocation, a lost generation like 2025) can hit the stock hard. The debate is less about whether AI-ASIC demand is real (it clearly is) and more about execution risk and customer concentration at a still-rich forward multiple.

risks.why_it_matters: Alchip openly states it has only ONE major hyperscaler accelerator account today; losing it, or that customer skipping a generation (as happened in 2025), would severely hit revenue.

risks.risk: Execution / yield on the N3 ramp
risks.why_it_matters: The 2026 thesis depends on the N3 accelerator ramping on time at good yield; any production or yield stumble directly cuts the expected recovery.
Upside is capped by how many scarce N3 wafers TSMC can supply (~6–7 month turnaround); capacity shortfalls limit shipments even when demand is strong.
Revenue and margins swing sharply between design-heavy and production-heavy phases per generation, making results volatile and hard to model.
Broadcom and Marvell are far bigger custom-silicon enablers; GUC, MediaTek, and Qualcomm also compete — pressuring win rates and pricing.
Hyperscalers may build more design capability in-house or split projects across vendors, limiting Alchip's share per design.

Automotive work is China-centric and engineering had been China-heavy; export controls or cross-strait tension could disrupt customers, talent, or supply (mitigated by diversifying engineering to Japan/Malaysia/Vietnam).
Even on forward earnings (~24x) the stock prices in a strong recovery; with a 52-week range of NT$2,480–5,640, disappointment can cause large drawdowns.
Demand depends on hyperscaler AI capex; a broad AI-spending digestion would slow accelerator programs and Alchip's ramp.
Gross margin falls as lower-margin production revenue grows; if pricing pressure exceeds plan, profit growth could lag revenue growth.

scenarios.disclaimer: Illustrative scenarios to frame the range of outcomes — NOT predictions, targets, or advice.

bull_case.thesis: The N3 accelerator ramps strongly and on time, full-year 2026 revenue surpasses the 2024 peak, the higher-value N2 generation scales in 2028, and Alchip adds a second major hyperscaler/networking account — turning a one-customer story into a diversified, multi-year grower.
key_drivers: N3 production ramps fast with good yield; Q3/Q4 2026 step up sharply; revenue beats the 2024 peak.
N2 chiplet NRE/ASP multiplies value capture; production scales 2028 with visibility to 2029.
Networking ASICs (>$100M/yr each) and automotive add diversification; a new hyperscaler account is won.
Forward P/E re-rates higher as the recovery and diversification de-risk the story.
bull_case.what_to_watch: Quarterly N3 production ramp; full-year vs 2024-peak revenue; N2 tape-out timing; new account wins; wafer/CoWoS allocation.

base_case.thesis: A solid, lumpy recovery: 2026 rebounds past the 2024 peak on the N3 ramp, margins normalize lower, and Alchip stays the leading neutral pure-play — but remains dependent on its one big accelerator customer and trades on execution quarter to quarter.
key_drivers: N3 production ramps roughly as guided; revenue back-end-loaded and above the 2024 peak.
Gross margin trends down as production grows; net profit still grows.
N2 progresses to a year-end tape-out; networking/automotive contribute steadily.
Stock tracks the earnings recovery at a still-premium forward multiple.
base_case.what_to_watch: Ramp linearity; margin trajectory; customer-concentration signals; competitive design wins/losses.

bear_case.thesis: Execution or customer issues repeat 2025: a yield problem, wafer-allocation shortfall, or a lost/delayed generation undercuts the ramp; with one dominant customer and a rich multiple, the small, volatile stock de-rates sharply.
key_drivers: N3 ramp slips on yield or wafer/CoWoS shortage; 2026 misses the 'above 2024 peak' bar.
The dominant customer in-sources, dual-sources, or skips a generation again.
Competition (Broadcom/Marvell/GUC) takes share on next designs; pricing pressure bites.
AI-capex digestion or geopolitics adds drag; the ~24x forward multiple compresses.

final_research_summary.one_paragraph: Alchip Technologies (3661.TW) is a Taiwan-listed, Cayman-incorporated PURE-PLAY ASIC design-service house — it engineers and manufactures the custom AI accelerators ('XPUs') that hyperscalers build to rival NVIDIA's GPUs, doing the leading-edge physical design and managing TSMC wafers + CoWoS + test. Its self-described edge is NEUTRALITY: it sells no chips or IP of its own, so the whole IP/optical/interconnect ecosystem will partner with it. The financial story is a clean trough-to-recovery: FY2025 (reported 2026-03-18) revenue fell ~39% to US$992M because the top customer skipped a product generation, yet net income held up far better (US$179.4M, EPS NT$69.2) thanks to a high-margin NRE mix; Q1 2026 (reported 2026-05-27) was the deliberate trough — revenue US$132.4M (-58.5% YoY) but a 50% gross margin and US$45.1M net income (EPS NT$17.55), with HPC 70% of sales. The inflection is now: the #1 customer's N3 AI accelerator began shipping ~June 2026 and ramps hard, so management guides a back-end-loaded year with full-year revenue expected to SURPASS the 2024 peak (~US$1.6B), the higher-value N2 chiplet generation taping out by end-2026 for ~2028 production, and visibility through 2029. On valuation, the stock (~NT$4,105, ~NT$335B / ~US$10.5B market cap, 52-week range NT$2,480–5,640) looks extreme on trailing earnings (~61x P/E at the trough) but reasonable on forward earnings (~24x), so it is priced as a recovery/growth story; consensus is 'Buy' (~23 analysts, avg target ~NT$5,733). What is FACT is a real, profitable, leading-edge custom-silicon franchise with secured N3/N2 programs; what is being PRICED is a flawless N3 ramp and continued reliance on essentially ONE dominant accelerator customer — so the core risks are execution and customer concentration, not whether the AI-ASIC wave is real.

AWS's ~$200B FY2026 capex is therefore a primary driver of demand for NVIDIA, Marvell, Broadcom, TSMC, the HBM makers, FormFactor (test), and the optical names (Coherent/Lumentum/AAOI) that wire its data centers. beginner_glossary.Amazon Web Services (AWS): Amazon's cloud-computing business — it rents computing power, storage, databases, and AI services to companies, governments, and startups over the internet. AWS is ~21% of Amazon's revenue but the majority of its profit, and it is the part of Amazon that matters most to the AI/semiconductor supply chain.
beginner_glossary.Cloud computing / hyperscaler: Instead of owning their own servers, companies rent computing from giant data-center operators ('hyperscalers') like AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. Hyperscalers are the biggest buyers of AI chips.
beginner_glossary.Segment (North America / International /: Amazon reports in three segments: North America (US/Canada retail + ads), International (other countries' retail + ads), and AWS (cloud). Profit is concentrated in AWS and, increasingly, advertising.
beginner_glossary.Capex (capital expenditure): Money spent building data centers, buying chips, servers, networking, power, and (for Amazon) fulfillment/robotics and satellites. Amazon plans ~$200B of capex in 2026, mostly for AWS/AI — a key driver of demand for the whole chip chain.
beginner_glossary.Custom silicon (Trainium / Inferentia /: Chips AWS designs itself (via its Annapurna Labs unit). Trainium = AI training/inference accelerator (competes with NVIDIA GPUs); Inferentia = inference chip; Graviton = Arm-based CPU. Designing its own chips lets AWS cut cost and reduce reliance on NVIDIA.
beginner_glossary.Annapurna Labs: The Amazon chip-design team (acquired 2015) behind Trainium, Inferentia, and Graviton.
beginner_glossary.GPU vs ASIC: A GPU (e.g., NVIDIA) is a flexible, off-the-shelf AI chip. An ASIC (like Trainium) is a custom chip tuned for specific work — often cheaper per unit of performance but less flexible. AWS uses BOTH.
beginner_glossary.Bedrock / SageMaker: AWS's AI platforms. Bedrock lets customers use many AI models (Anthropic's Claude, Meta's Llama, Mistral, and now OpenAI) as a managed service; SageMaker is for building/training models. Bedrock is a major AWS AI growth driver.
beginner_glossary.Agentic AI / agent: AI that doesn't just answer once but reasons, plans, and uses tools to do multi-step work. AWS sells agent tools (Strands, AgentCore, Quro/Qwik) and says agents will drive most AI value — and lots of CPU demand (hence Graviton).
beginner_glossary.Anthropic / OpenAI: Leading AI 'labs' (model makers). Amazon is Anthropic's largest investor and signed a >$100B AWS deal with it; OpenAI's models are now on Bedrock. Both made multi-gigawatt training commitments — huge future AWS revenue.
beginner_glossary.Backlog (RPO): Contracted future revenue not yet recognized ('remaining performance obligations'). AWS's backlog was $364B in Q1 2026 — a measure of demand visibility (and that figure excludes the recent >$100B Anthropic deal).
beginner_glossary.Annualized run rate: A quarter's revenue multiplied to a yearly pace. AWS is at a ~$150B annualized run rate; AWS's custom-chip business is at a >$20B run rate (>$50B if it sold all its chips externally).
beginner_glossary.Operating income vs net income: Operating income = profit from running the business (the cleanest operational gauge). Net income = the bottom line after interest, taxes, and gains/losses on investments (Amazon's net income swings with the value of stakes like Anthropic and Rivian).
beginner_glossary.Operating margin: Operating income ÷ revenue. Amazon hit a record 13.1% companywide; AWS alone runs ~37.7% — which is why AWS drives most of the profit.
beginner_glossary.Advertising: Amazon sells ads (sponsored products, Prime Video ads, etc.) — a fast-growing, high-margin business that cleared a >$70B trailing run rate.
beginner_glossary.Prime: Amazon's paid membership (fast shipping, Prime Video, etc.) that drives loyalty and spending.
beginner_glossary.Free cash flow (FCF) / ROIC: FCF = cash left after capex. ROIC = return on invested capital. Amazon's FCF is being SQUEEZED right now because AI capex is growing faster than revenue; management argues the long-run ROIC is attractive once the new capacity is monetized.
beginner_glossary.Memory / HBM cost: Memory chips (DRAM/HBM) have spiked in price due to AI demand. Amazon flagged this as a cost/capex pressure — and it links AWS to memory makers (SK Hynix/Samsung/Micron).
beginner_glossary.Amazon LEO: Amazon's low-earth-orbit satellite network (formerly 'Project Kuiper') for broadband — capital-intensive, launching commercially in 2026; a newer, separate growth bet.
beginner_glossary.P/E and P/S: P/E = price ÷ earnings per share; P/S = market value ÷ revenue. Amazon trades ~28x earnings and ~3.5x sales — far more grounded than the small-cap AI names, because its profits are large and real.

For THIS supply-chain graph, the relevant node is AWS, the hyperscaler that buys and builds AI chips and hosts AI labs.

business_model.summary: Amazon makes money three ways: renting cloud computing (AWS), selling/【facilitating retail (its own goods + a huge third-party marketplace + Prime + grocery), and selling advertising. Retail drives enormous revenue at thin margins; AWS and advertising drive most of the profit. The current story is AWS reaccelerating on AI demand while Amazon pours ~$200B of capex into AI infrastructure (including its own chips) — pressuring near-term free cash flow but, management argues, building very large future revenue and returns.
how_they_make_money: AWS (cloud): renting compute, storage, databases, networking, and AI services (Bedrock, SageMaker). $37.6B in Q1 2026 (+28% YoY) at a ~37.7% operating margin — the profit engine.
North America retail: 1P (own inventory) + 3P marketplace fees + Prime subscriptions + grocery (now the #2 US grocer) + devices. $104.1B in Q1 2026 (+12%).
International retail: the same model outside the US. $39.8B in Q1 2026 (+11% ex-FX).
Advertising: sponsored products, Prime Video ads, etc. $17.2B in Q1 2026 (+22%); a high-margin, >$70B trailing business.

Custom silicon: Trainium/Inferentia/Graviton cut AWS's own costs (expected to save 'tens of billions of capex per year') and are increasingly sold to external customers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Uber).
competitive_moat_analyst_view: AWS scale + breadth: the broadest, most-adopted cloud, with deep security/operational track record — customers keep their AI inference near their data, which lives in AWS. [Q1 2026 call]
Full chip stack (Trainium + Graviton): owning both the leading price-performance AI accelerator and the leading Arm CPU is a structural cost and margin advantage few rivals match. [Q1 2026 call]
AI-lab anchor tenants: Anthropic (largest investor; >$100B deal) and OpenAI (models on Bedrock) anchor demand and validate Trainium. [Q1 2026 call]
Retail flywheel + Prime + logistics: scale, selection, fast delivery, and a >$70B ads business create a hard-to-replicate consumer moat. [Q1 2026 call]
Capital + know-how to fund ~$200B/year of AI infrastructure — a barrier only a few companies can clear. [Q1 2026 call]

revenue_streams.analyst_view: Amazon is a retail giant with two profit engines (AWS and advertising). AWS is ~21% of revenue but the majority of operating income and essentially all of the AI story; advertising (~9%) is the fast-growing, high-margin sweetener; retail (~79% of revenue) provides scale and cash but thin margins. For this graph, AWS is what matters — and its 28% reacceleration plus the $364B backlog and Trainium commitments are the key signals. The companywide record 13.1% operating margin shows the mix is shifting toward the profitable businesses.

final_research_summary.one_paragraph: Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN; graph node 'Amazon Web Services') is a ~$2.6T mega-cap with three businesses — AWS (cloud), retail/marketplace, and advertising — but for this AI/semiconductor supply chain the relevant node is AWS, the hyperscaler that buys NVIDIA GPUs, builds its own Trainium/Graviton chips, and hosts the AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI). The quarter was strong: Q1 2026 (reported 2026-04-29) revenue was $181.5B (+17% YoY) with a RECORD 13.1% operating margin ($23.9B operating income), and the standout was AWS reaccelerating to $37.6B (+28% YoY, a 15-quarter high) at a ~37.7% margin and a ~$150B run rate, with a $364B backlog that EXCLUDES a recent >$100B Anthropic deal. AWS's custom-silicon business is now a 'top-3 data-center chip business' (>$20B run rate, >$50B if sold fully externally) with >$225B of Trainium commitments, even as Amazon keeps buying substantial NVIDIA GPUs — classic hyperscaler 'co-opetition.' The central tension is capital: Amazon plans ~$200B of capex in FY2026 (mostly AWS/AI), which is growing faster than revenue and CONSTRAINING free cash flow now; management argues (and the backlog/commitments support) that this builds very large future revenue and attractive multi-year ROIC, but that won't be proven until the capacity is monetized. On valuation, Amazon is far more grounded than the small-cap AI names — ~28x trailing earnings and ~3.5x sales — and analysts are strongly bullish (Strong Buy; ~$313 average target, ~30% above the ~$239 price). The facts (record margins, AWS reacceleration, $364B+ backlog, Trainium scale, ads >$70B) are strong and well-documented; what is debated is the RETURN on ~$200B/year of AI capex and the durability of AWS growth against Azure/Google Cloud. The core debate is capex-ROI + AWS durability, not whether Amazon is a quality, cash-generative franchise.

beginner_glossary.CPU vs GPU: A CPU (central processing unit) is the general-purpose 'brain' that runs most software and orchestrates tasks; a GPU (graphics processing unit) does massively parallel math and is the workhorse for AI training/inference. AMD is one of very few companies that makes BOTH at the leading edge.
beginner_glossary.EPYC: AMD's brand of server (data-center) CPUs — its share-gaining product line versus Intel's Xeon. Newer generations: Genoa (Zen 4), Turin (Zen 5), and upcoming Venice (Zen 6, 2nm).
beginner_glossary.Instinct (MI300 / MI350 / MI355X / MI450: AMD's brand of AI-accelerator GPUs that compete with NVIDIA's. MI350/MI355X are shipping now; MI450 (with the 'Helios' rack system) ramps in 2H 2026; MI500 is the next generation. This is AMD's bid to be the #2 AI-GPU supplier.
beginner_glossary.Helios (rack-scale): AMD's full AI server 'rack' that integrates Instinct GPUs + EPYC CPUs + networking into one optimized system — competing with NVIDIA's rack-scale platforms. Production ramps in 2H 2026.
beginner_glossary.ROCm: AMD's software stack for running AI on its GPUs — the equivalent of NVIDIA's CUDA. AMD is investing heavily here because software maturity is key to winning GPU customers.
beginner_glossary.Ryzen: AMD's PC CPUs (laptops/desktops), including AI PC chips (Ryzen AI). The Client segment's main product, gaining share versus Intel.
beginner_glossary.Radeon: AMD's gaming/graphics GPUs (e.g., Radeon 9000 series), competing with NVIDIA's GeForce.
beginner_glossary.Semi-custom: Custom chips AMD designs for specific customers — most famously the processors inside PlayStation and Xbox consoles. Part of the Gaming segment; cyclical with console generations.
beginner_glossary.Embedded / FPGA (Xilinx): Chips for industrial, aerospace/defense, communications, and test equipment — largely from AMD's 2022 acquisition of Xilinx. FPGAs are reconfigurable chips; 'adaptive' computing. A higher-margin, steadier segment.
beginner_glossary.Zen architecture (Zen 4 / 5 / 6): AMD's CPU design generations. Each Zen step improves performance and efficiency; Venice (Zen 6) is built on a 2-nanometer process.
beginner_glossary.Venice / Verano / Turin / Genoa / Milan: AMD EPYC server-CPU generations/names. Turin (current) crossed >50% of server revenue; Venice (next, Zen 6/2nm) launches later in 2026; Verano is a Venice-family CPU purpose-built for AI infrastructure.
beginner_glossary.Fabless: AMD designs chips but does NOT own factories — TSMC manufactures them. This keeps AMD asset-light but dependent on TSMC capacity.
beginner_glossary.HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory): Stacked fast memory placed on AI GPUs. AMD's Instinct chips emphasize large HBM capacity/bandwidth as an advantage, especially for inference. AMD buys HBM from SK Hynix/Samsung/Micron.
beginner_glossary.Inference vs training: Training = teaching an AI model (very GPU-heavy); inference = running the trained model to answer requests. Inference is the larger, faster-growing workload, and AMD highlights its memory advantage there.
beginner_glossary.Agentic AI: AI that plans and acts in multiple steps ('agents'). It spawns many sub-tasks that need CPU compute (orchestration, data movement) — AMD's reason for sharply raising its server-CPU market forecast.
beginner_glossary.CPU-to-GPU ratio: How many GPUs pair with each CPU in AI servers. AMD says it's moving from ~1:4-1:8 toward ~1:1 (or more CPUs) as workloads turn agentic — meaning MORE CPU demand per AI cluster.
beginner_glossary.TAM (Total Addressable Market): The total size of a market. AMD raised its 2030 server-CPU TAM estimate to over $120B (from ~$60B), and targets >50% share.
beginner_glossary.Sovereign AI: AI infrastructure built by governments/nations for their own use — a growing Instinct customer category.
beginner_glossary.MLPerf: An industry AI-performance benchmark; AMD cited leadership results for its MI355X in several categories.
beginner_glossary.P/E ratio (Price-to-Earnings): Share price divided by yearly earnings per share. AMD's ~170x trailing (GAAP) / ~59x forward P/E is high, reflecting big expected earnings growth from the AI ramp.

final_research_summary.one_paragraph: AMD (Advanced Micro Devices) is the only company credibly challenging two giants at once: it is the #2 AI-accelerator maker chasing NVIDIA, and the #2 — and share-gaining — x86 CPU maker versus Intel. Under CEO Lisa Su it has become a data-center powerhouse. Q1 2026 (reported 2026-05-05) was outstanding: revenue $10.3B (+38% YoY), record Data Center revenue $5.8B (+57%), non-GAAP gross margin 55%, non-GAAP EPS $1.37 (+43%), and record free cash flow $2.6B. The company sharply RAISED its 2030 server-CPU market forecast to over $120B (from ~$60B) on agentic-AI CPU demand, targets >50% server-CPU share, and aims for 'tens of billions of dollars' of annual Data Center AI revenue in 2027 — underpinned by multi-generation, multi-gigawatt Instinct deals with Meta (up to 6 GW) and OpenAI, with the MI450 GPU and Helios rack-scale system ramping in 2H 2026. FY2025 was a record (revenue $34.6B; non-GAAP EPS $4.17; Data Center $16.6B, +32%). Valuation is rich — the stock has run ~4.5x in a year to ~$511.57 (a ~$834B market cap), ~59x forward earnings and ~22x sales — but, crucially, it is backed by a profitable, fast-growing business (TTM net income +125% to $5.01B), and analysts are 'Strong Buy' with an average target ($486) roughly at the current price. So what is FACT is a real, accelerating, cash-generative franchise gaining share in CPUs and inflecting in AI GPUs; what is being PRICED is AMD successfully scaling Instinct to 'tens of billions' by 2027 against NVIDIA's dominance AND continued EPYC share gains. The central debate is how big a #2 AMD becomes in AI accelerators — not whether the business is healthy (it clearly is).

beginner_glossary.OSAT (Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly: A company that does the BACK-END of chipmaking for others: after a foundry makes the bare silicon, the OSAT assembles it into a finished 'package' (protecting the chip and connecting it to a circuit board) and tests it. Amkor is the world's #2 OSAT (behind ASE). It owns no chip designs — it is a contract service provider, like a foundry but for packaging/test.
beginner_glossary.Packaging (semiconductor): Turning a bare silicon die into a usable chip — encasing it, wiring its connections, and (increasingly) combining multiple dies + memory into one module. 'Advanced packaging' does the complex, high-value versions needed for AI and high-performance computing.
beginner_glossary.Advanced vs mainstream packaging: Mainstream = simpler, lower-price packages (e.g., wire bond) for everyday chips. Advanced = complex, high-value packages (flip chip, fan-out, 2.5D) for AI/compute, premium phones, and advanced cars. Amkor's profit growth comes from mix-shifting toward advanced.
beginner_glossary.Wire bond / flip chip: Two ways to connect a chip to its package. Wire bond (older, cheaper) uses tiny wires; flip chip (newer) flips the chip onto bumps for faster, denser connections. Flip chip is a building block of advanced packaging.
beginner_glossary.HDFO (High-Density Fan-Out): Amkor's family of advanced packages that spread a chip's connections out over a larger area without a bulky substrate — key for AI/HPC chips. Amkor's HDFO platforms include SWIFT and S-Connect / Amkor-Connect.
beginner_glossary.SWIFT / S-Connect / Amkor-Connect: Amkor's branded advanced-packaging technologies. Management compares SWIFT to TSMC's CoWoS-R and S-Connect to TSMC's CoWoS-L — i.e., they are outsourced alternatives to the foundry's in-house AI packaging.
beginner_glossary.2.5D / silicon interposer: An advanced package where multiple chips (e.g., a processor + HBM memory) sit side-by-side on a silicon 'interposer' that wires them together at high speed. The standard way AI accelerators are built.
beginner_glossary.CoWoS (TSMC) — for comparison: TSMC's flagship in-house advanced-packaging method for AI chips. Because CoWoS capacity is scarce, customers increasingly want OUTSOURCED alternatives — which is Amkor's opportunity.
beginner_glossary.HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory): Stacked DRAM placed next to AI processors. Amkor packages chips that integrate HBM; HBM/'advanced silicon' supply timing affects Amkor's loading.
beginner_glossary.Test: Checking that finished chips work to spec. Amkor offers test alongside packaging; it is a higher-value, sticky service.
beginner_glossary.End markets (Communications / Computing: Amkor reports revenue by where the chips go. Communications = smartphones (big Apple/iOS exposure); Computing = PCs + AI data center; Automotive & Industrial = cars (ADAS, infotainment) + industrial; Consumer = wearables, etc.
beginner_glossary.Utilization: How full Amkor's factories are running. Higher utilization spreads fixed costs over more units, lifting margins (Q1 2026 was in the low-70s%, up from the 50s a year earlier).
beginner_glossary.Operating leverage: Because factories have high fixed costs, each extra dollar of revenue at higher utilization drops a larger share to profit — why Amkor's margins jump when demand is strong.
beginner_glossary.Gross margin (OSAT context): OSAT gross margins are structurally LOW (Amkor ~14-15%) versus a foundry's (TSMC ~66%), because packaging is more labor/equipment-intensive and less differentiated than wafer-making. So Amkor's profit story is about VOLUME, utilization, and mix-shift to advanced — not high margins per unit.
beginner_glossary.EBITDA: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — a cash-earnings gauge. Amkor's Q1 2026 EBITDA was $285M (16.9% margin); useful because Amkor is capital-intensive (lots of depreciation).
beginner_glossary.CapEx / capital intensity: Money spent on factories and equipment. Amkor is capital-intensive (2026 CapEx guided $2.5-3.0B on ~$7B+ revenue) because packaging needs constant new tools and buildings.
beginner_glossary.Arizona facility / CHIPS Act / ITC: Amkor's new U.S. advanced-packaging campus near TSMC's Arizona fabs. A ~$7B two-phase project, supported by a $400M U.S. CHIPS Act grant and a 35% investment tax credit (~$2.8B combined). Phase 1 completes 2027, production 2028, scaling to full impact by 2030.
beginner_glossary.Partnership / co-investment model: Amkor's customers (foundries, fabless, IDMs) increasingly help fund its capacity (prepayments, capital support) in exchange for guaranteed supply — reducing Amkor's investment risk and aligning roadmaps.
beginner_glossary.P/E ratio (Price-to-Earnings): Share price divided by yearly earnings per share. Amkor's ~48x trailing / ~38x forward P/E is HIGH for an OSAT (which historically traded ~15-20x), reflecting big AI-packaging growth expectations.

company_snapshot.what_it_is: Amkor Technology is the world's #2 outsourced semiconductor assembly-and-test company (OSAT) and the leading independent (non-foundry) provider of ADVANCED packaging for AI/high-performance computing, premium smartphones, and advanced automotive chips. After a foundry makes the silicon, Amkor turns it into a finished, tested package. It is increasingly a key 'second source' for advanced AI packaging as in-house foundry capacity (e.g., TSMC's CoWoS) stays scarce.
company_snapshot.founder_ceo: Founded by James J. Kim; the Kim family retains majority control. Led by President & CEO Kevin Engel; EVP & CFO Megan Faust (both presented the Q1 2026 call).
company_snapshot.manufacturing_footprint: Global, with the most advanced packaging in Korea and Taiwan; mainstream/assembly in the Philippines, Vietnam, Japan, and China; and a new U.S. advanced-packaging campus under construction in Arizona (Phase 1 completion 2027, production 2028). A new Korea test building completes end-2026; SiP production is migrating from Korea to Vietnam to free advanced capacity. [Q1 2026 call, 2026-04-27]

business_model.summary: Amkor makes money by providing outsourced packaging and test services and charging per unit, with much higher value for advanced packages than mainstream ones. Its profit lever is operating leverage: fill the factories (utilization), shift the mix toward advanced packaging, and push pricing — and margins expand. The current driver is AI: as chips get more complex and CoWoS-type capacity stays scarce, customers turn to Amkor's advanced platforms (HDFO/2.5D), and Amkor's advanced-AI-packaging revenue is guided to TRIPLE in 2026.
how_they_make_money: Advanced packaging — flip chip, HDFO (SWIFT, S-Connect), and 2.5D/silicon-interposer for AI/HPC, premium phones, and advanced auto. The high-value, fastest-growing part of the mix. [Q1 2026 call]
Mainstream packaging — wire-bond and simpler packages for everyday chips (autos' drivetrain, industrial, consumer). Lower-value but recovering (4 straight quarters of growth). [Q1 2026 call]
Test services — verifying finished chips work; a higher-value, sticky add-on to packaging.
Foundry/turnkey collaboration — outsourced work tied to foundry and IDM partners (e.g., a collaboration with Intel related to EMIB packaging). [Q1 2026 call]
competitive_moat_analyst_view: Scale + advanced-packaging leadership: the #2 OSAT overall and the leading INDEPENDENT advanced-packaging provider, with HDFO/2.5D platforms qualified at a broadening customer base (5+ on HDFO; half-a-dozen-plus on 2.5D). [Q1 2026 call]

Customer trust + partnership model: deep ties with foundries, fabless leaders, IDMs and OEMs, with customers CO-FUNDING capacity (prepayments/capital support) — de-risking Amkor's investment and locking in demand. [Q1 2026 call]
Geographic footprint incl. the U.S.: the Arizona campus (CHIPS-funded, near TSMC Arizona) positions Amkor as the leading U.S. advanced-packaging partner as supply chains regionalize. [Q1 2026 call]
Second-source value: with foundry in-house packaging (CoWoS) scarce, Amkor is the natural outsourced alternative — customers are 'very motivated' to qualify it quickly. [Q1 2026 call]
facts: Q1 2026: record Q1 revenue $1.68B (+27% YoY), EPS $0.33, gross margin 14.2%, operating margin 6% (+360bps YoY); utilization low-70s% (vs 50s a year earlier). [Q1 2026 call, 2026-04-27]
Advanced AI-packaging revenue guided to TRIPLE in 2026; computing end market guided ~+20% for the full year. [Q1 2026 call]
Arizona: ~$7B two-phase campus; $400M CHIPS grant + 35% ITC (~$2.8B support); production 2028, full impact by 2030; ~$1B revenue run-rate potential (>10% of 2025 revenue). [Q1 2026 call]

revenue_streams.analyst_view: Two engines are running: a near-term cyclical recovery (communications/Apple strength, auto advanced, rising utilization) and a structural AI advanced-packaging ramp (computing +20%, AI packaging tripling, the new data-center CPU). The mix-shift toward advanced packaging plus higher utilization is lifting margins off a low base. The catch is that revenue can be 'nonlinear' quarter-to-quarter because customer material (advanced silicon/memory/substrates) sometimes slips, pushing demand around.

industry_trends.trend: AI is moving value into advanced packaging
industry_trends.why_it_matters: As transistor scaling slows, stitching chips together (advanced packaging) is where performance gains and value increasingly come from — directly Amkor's domain.
industry_trends.evidence: Management: 'the semiconductor industry turns to advanced packaging for value creation'; advanced AI-packaging revenue guided to triple in 2026; 'multiyear value creation journey.' [Q1 2026 call, 2026-04-27]

industry_trends.trend: Scarce in-house foundry packaging (CoWoS) drives outsourcing to OSATs
industry_trends.why_it_matters: When TSMC's CoWoS is sold out, customers need a qualified second source — Amkor's HDFO/2.5D platforms — accelerating its AI engagements.
industry_trends.evidence: HDFO platforms (SWIFT ~ CoWoS-R; S-Connect ~ CoWoS-L) now engaged with 5+ customers; 2.5D interposer with half-a-dozen-plus; customers 'very motivated' to qualify quickly. [Q1 2026 call]

industry_trends.why_it_matters: Tight advanced silicon, advanced substrates, and memory can delay customer materials, pushing Amkor's revenue around quarter-to-quarter (a risk to linear growth).
industry_trends.evidence: Management: forecasted wafers/memory sometimes don't show up; estimated a ~$50-100M material-supply pushout impact in Q1, with a similar level expected in Q2. [Q1 2026 call]

industry_trends.why_it_matters: Regionalizing the supply chain creates a U.S. advanced-packaging opportunity next to TSMC's Arizona fabs, partly government-funded.
industry_trends.evidence: Arizona: ~$7B two phases; $400M CHIPS grant + 35% ITC (~$2.8B); Phase 1 completion 2027, production 2028, full impact 2030; will dilute operating margin ~1-2% in 2027 before becoming accretive. [Q1 2026 call]

industry_trends.why_it_matters: Rising precious-metal/commodity and gas prices raise Amkor's input costs; it must offset via pricing.
industry_trends.evidence: Management cites Middle East-driven pricing pressure on materials; a 'constructive pricing environment' lets Amkor work with customers to recover most cost increases through the year. [Q1 2026 call]

industry_trends.trend: Memory price surge rippling through the chain
industry_trends.why_it_matters: High memory prices and prioritization affect customer build plans and Amkor's loading mix (it packages many memory-adjacent chips).
industry_trends.evidence: Management: customers are prioritizing/seeking optionality around memory supply; hard to gauge exact demand impact, but overall demand remains strong. [Q1 2026 call]

competitors.landscape_summary: Packaging/test is split between independent OSATs and the foundries/IDMs that do packaging in-house. Among OSATs, ASE is #1 and Amkor #2, with several Chinese players (JCET, TongFu) and Taiwan's Powertech in the field. Separately, the big foundries (TSMC, Samsung, Intel) do their own advanced packaging — so Amkor both competes with and complements them, increasingly winning OUTSOURCED advanced work as foundry capacity is constrained.

competitors.differentiation_analyst_view: Amkor's edge is being the leading INDEPENDENT advanced-packaging provider — the natural outsourced second source when foundry packaging is full — plus a U.S. footprint (Arizona) that ASE and Chinese rivals lack at the leading edge. Its risks: ASE is bigger; the foundries could keep more advanced packaging in-house; and Chinese OSATs compete hard on price in mainstream.

financial_performance.analyst_view: Amkor is inflecting: +27% Q1 revenue, gross margin and operating margin both expanding off a low base, utilization rising from the 50s to the low-70s, and an AI advanced-packaging ramp guided to triple. The balance sheet (1.1x debt/EBITDA, $2.9B liquidity) comfortably funds the build. Two honest caveats: (1) OSAT margins are structurally thin (gross ~14-15%), so this is a volume/operating-leverage story, not a high-margin one; and (2) Arizona will be a near-term (2027) margin drag before it pays off later in the decade.

valuation.analyst_view: Valuation is the hardest part of the AMKR story. The operational inflection is real (AI packaging tripling, margins expanding, Arizona optionality), but the stock has re-rated ~4x in a year to ~48x trailing earnings for a structurally thin-margin OSAT — and it now trades ABOVE the average analyst target. That combination means the price already embeds a lot of the AI-packaging growth; disappointment on the AI ramp, Arizona timing, or memory/material supply could de-rate it (the 52-week low was $19.79). The May 21 Investor Day's long-range targets are the key catalyst for whether the multiple is justified.

risks.why_it_matters: At ~48x trailing / ~38x forward earnings for a thin-margin OSAT — and trading ABOVE the average analyst target — the stock prices in years of AI-packaging growth; disappointment could de-rate it hard (52-week low $19.79).
A large share of revenue depends on premium-smartphone (iOS) packaging; a shift in that customer's volumes, supply-chain choices, or share would be material.
The 'tripling' depends on advanced-silicon, substrate, and memory supply plus Amkor's own equipment ramp; material slips already cause ~$50-100M/quarter of 'nonlinear' pushouts.
A ~$7B build that dilutes operating margin ~1-2% in 2027 before paying off later; delays, qualification slips, or weak loading would hurt returns.
Gross margins ~14-15% leave little cushion; the model needs high utilization and mix-shift to work, and downturns hit operating leverage in reverse.
Packaging volumes track the broader chip cycle; an AI-capex pause or consumer-demand slump would cut utilization and margins.
ASE is larger; Chinese OSATs press on price; and foundries (TSMC/Samsung/Intel) could keep more advanced packaging in-house, shrinking the outsourced pool.
Middle East-driven commodity/precious-metal and gas costs pressure margins; tariffs and export controls add demand/supply uncertainty.
Sustained $2.5-3.0B CapEx on ~$7B revenue consumes cash and raises execution risk if demand softens after the spend.
The Kim family's majority control limits outside-shareholder influence over strategy and capital allocation.

final_research_summary.one_paragraph: Amkor Technology (AMKR) is the world's #2 outsourced semiconductor assembly-and-test company (OSAT) and the leading INDEPENDENT provider of advanced packaging — the back-end step that turns a foundry's silicon into a finished, tested chip, and increasingly stitches AI processors together with HBM memory. It sits in the packaging tier of the AI supply chain (one step after TSMC) and is a natural 'second source' as in-house foundry packaging (CoWoS) stays scarce. The business is inflecting: Q1 2026 (reported 2026-04-27) delivered record Q1 revenue of $1.68B (+27% YoY) with EPS of $0.33 (a ~40% beat), gross margin 14.2%, operating margin up 360bps to 6%, and utilization rising from the 50s to the low-70s — and management guides advanced AI-packaging revenue to TRIPLE in 2026, with computing up ~20%. It is also building a ~$7B U.S. advanced-packaging campus in Arizona (with ~$2.8B of CHIPS-grant + tax-credit support) that should scale to full impact by 2030. The balance sheet is healthy (1.1x debt/EBITDA, $2.9B liquidity). The catch is valuation: the stock has re-rated ~4x in a year to ~$83 (an all-time high) and ~$20.5B market cap, trading at ~48x trailing / ~38x forward earnings for a structurally thin-margin OSAT (gross margin ~14-15%) — and it now sits ABOVE the average analyst price target of $75.50. So what is FACT is a genuine AI-packaging-led inflection with expanding margins and a funded U.S. growth project; what is being PRICED is years of that growth compounding flawlessly. The key debates are the AI ramp's durability/linearity and the rich multiple — not whether Amkor is well-positioned in advanced packaging. Watch the May 21 Investor Day for the long-range targets that must justify the valuation.

It is in a heavy CONSTRUCTION phase, so it is currently loss-making and a normal P/E is meaningless. The right lens is real-estate/infrastructure style: contracted lease backlog, NOI (net operating income), EBITDA, the credit quality of its tenants, and its cost of capital.

report_meta.supply_chain_link: Applied Digital sits in the DATA-CENTER/INFRASTRUCTURE layer of the AI supply chain — the physical buildings, power, and cooling that house the GPUs. It LEASES capacity to AI compute providers; its biggest tenant is the neocloud CoreWeave, and it is signing investment-grade hyperscalers. Its demand is the same hyperscaler AI-capex wave that drives NVIDIA, TSMC, the memory makers, and the power names (see reports/NVIDIA.json, reports/Monolithic Power Systems.json).

beginner_glossary.AI / HPC data center: A large, specialized building that houses the servers and GPUs that run AI and high-performance computing. Applied Digital builds and operates these and rents them out.
beginner_glossary.Critical IT load (megawatt / MW / gigawa: Data centers are measured by their POWER capacity, not floor space. 1 MW powers roughly a building's worth of AI servers; 1 GW = 1,000 MW (a giant campus). Applied Digital talks about hundreds of MW now and a path to 5-6 GW over time.
beginner_glossary.Direct-to-chip liquid cooling: Cooling AI chips with liquid piped right to the chip (instead of air), needed because AI GPUs run extremely hot. Applied Digital operates one of the few 100 MW liquid-cooled AI data centers online today.
beginner_glossary.Hyperscaler: A giant cloud company (e.g., Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, Oracle) that needs enormous data-center capacity. Applied Digital wants to sign long-term leases with these (and is targeting an investment-grade one).
beginner_glossary.Neocloud (e.g., CoreWeave): A newer, specialized AI-cloud company that rents out GPUs. CoreWeave is Applied Digital's biggest tenant. Neoclouds are fast-growing but younger and more leveraged than hyperscalers — so their credit quality matters a lot to a landlord.
beginner_glossary.Lease / contracted backlog: Applied Digital signs long-term (15-30 year) leases to rent its data centers. The 'contracted backlog' (~$16B) is the total future rent already signed — the foundation of its value. Leases are 'take-or-pay': the tenant owes rent even if it doesn't use the space.
beginner_glossary.NOI (Net Operating Income): Rental income minus the direct costs of running the property — the key profit measure for infrastructure/real estate. Applied Digital targets $1B+ of annual NOI within five years. Its site NOI margins are very high (high-80s to 90s% on a cash basis).
beginner_glossary.Adjusted EBITDA: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (adjusted) — a cash-earnings proxy. Q3 FY2026 was $44.1M as the first building leased up.
beginner_glossary.SPV (Special Purpose Vehicle): A separate legal entity used to isolate and finance a specific project or lease. Applied Digital restructured its CoreWeave leases through a CoreWeave-owned SPV that earned an investment-grade rating.
beginner_glossary.Investment-grade credit rating (A3 vs BB: A measure of how safe a borrower/tenant is. 'Investment grade' (e.g., A3) is much safer (and cheaper to finance) than 'below investment grade' (e.g., BB). The CoreWeave lease SPV jumping from BB to A3 lowers Applied Digital's borrowing costs.
beginner_glossary.Cost of capital / ABS / project finance: The interest rate Applied Digital pays to fund construction. It uses project-finance loans now (higher cost) and plans to refinance into ABS (asset-backed securities) markets at lower rates once buildings are de-risked — management calls this the 'tipping point' for shareholder returns.
beginner_glossary.Preferred equity (Macquarie): A type of financing between debt and common stock. Applied Digital has access to $4.1B of preferred equity from Macquarie (per an executed investment-grade lease) to fund new sites while keeping >80% common ownership.
beginner_glossary.RFS (Ready For Service): The date a data-center building is energized and starts generating lease revenue. Buildings energize gradually (data hall by data hall) over a few months.
beginner_glossary.Polaris Forge / Delta Forge: Applied Digital's campus names. Polaris Forge 1 (Ellendale, North Dakota) is the 400 MW CoreWeave campus; Polaris Forge 2 is a 200 MW investment-grade-hyperscaler campus; Delta Forge 1 is a new 300 MW campus in the Southern U.S. (operational ~mid-2027).
beginner_glossary.Grid power vs behind-the-meter: 'Grid power' = electricity from the public utility grid (preferred by hyperscalers, reliable). 'Behind-the-meter / on-site generation' = building your own power plant at the site. Applied Digital prioritizes grid power — a selling point versus rivals relying on on-site gas.
beginner_glossary.ChronoScale (Cloud spin-off): Applied Digital is separating its GPU-Cloud business and combining it with Exo Bionic to form ChronoScale Corporation, intended to be spun off to shareholders — so APLD becomes a purer data-center landlord.
beginner_glossary.Base Electron (IPP): An independent power producer Applied Digital is supporting (with Babcock & Wilcox) to add ~1.2 GW of natural-gas grid power in the Dakotas. Structured OUTSIDE Applied Digital to avoid power-plant risk; APLD shareholders get ~10% upside.
beginner_glossary.Bitcoin / crypto hosting (data center se: Applied Digital's legacy business hosting Bitcoin miners. It is small but the highest-return, cash-generative segment today.
beginner_glossary.Leverage (x NOI) / escalators: How much debt is used, measured against NOI. Applied Digital targets a prudent 5-6x NOI (vs private peers >10x). 'Escalators' are built-in annual rent increases in the leases.

company_snapshot.what_it_is: Applied Digital is a developer, owner, and operator of large-scale AI/HPC data centers — the physical 'AI factories' (power + buildings + liquid cooling) that house GPUs. It signs long-term (15-30 year) leases with AI compute providers (its biggest tenant is the neocloud CoreWeave, and it is adding investment-grade hyperscalers). It also runs a small, cash-generative legacy crypto-hosting business and is spinning off its GPU-Cloud unit (as 'ChronoScale'). The thesis: turn a ~$16B contracted lease backlog into a $1B+ annual NOI annuity stream as its campuses are built and financed cheaply.
company_snapshot.founder_ceo: Chairman & CEO: Wes Cummins. CFO: Saidal Mohmand.
company_snapshot.founded: ~2020 (celebrated its five-year anniversary in 2026)
company_snapshot.operating_footprint: Core campuses in North Dakota — Polaris Forge 1 (Ellendale, 400 MW, CoreWeave) and Polaris Forge 2 (200 MW), plus a third ND site — chosen for low-cost power and cold climate. Expanding to the Southern U.S. (Delta Forge 1, 300 MW) and marketing four development sites totaling ~1 GW. ~900 MW under construction. [Q3 FY2026 call, 2026-04-08]
end_markets: AI/HPC data-center leasing to neoclouds (CoreWeave) and hyperscalers
GPU cloud (being spun off as ChronoScale)

business_model.summary: Applied Digital makes money by building AI data centers and renting them out under long-term leases — collecting rent (and high-margin NOI) for 15-30 years from creditworthy tenants. It is essentially an AI-infrastructure landlord. Today it is in a capital-intensive BUILD phase (hence current losses), funding construction with project debt and preferred equity. The value unlock comes as buildings energize (revenue ramps) and as it refinances expensive construction debt into cheaper long-term debt — the point at which management says shareholder returns 'significantly ramp.'
how_they_make_money: HPC hosting (the future): long-term leases on AI data centers. Q3 FY2026 HPC revenue $71M = $44.1M base rent + $18.9M tenant fit-out + $8.1M power pass-through/other; segment operating profit $17.6M. [Q3 FY2026 call]
Data center hosting (crypto): hosting Bitcoin miners — small but the HIGHEST-return segment. Q3 FY2026 revenue $37.5M (+7% YoY), operating profit $13.9M on just $119.6M of assets. [Q3 FY2026 call]
Cloud (being separated): GPU-cloud business, consolidated for now ($18.1M revenue in Q3) but merging with Exo Bionic into ChronoScale to be spun off to shareholders. [Q3 FY2026 call]
Future upside: equity stakes in adjacent ventures — ~10% of Base Electron (power) and the ChronoScale spin — give shareholders optionality outside the core landlord business.
competitive_moat_analyst_view: First-mover execution at scale: one of the only 100 MW direct-to-chip liquid-cooled AI data centers online today, with proven ability to build through North Dakota winters on time/on budget — a credibility edge with hyperscalers. [Q3 FY2026 call]

Low-cost, well-located GRID power: campuses in the Dakotas with cheap power and cold climate, prioritizing grid power (preferred by hyperscalers) over on-site generation — scarce, premium assets as power becomes the binding constraint. [Q3 FY2026 call]

$16B contracted backlog + financing structure: long-dated leases plus a CoreWeave SPV upgraded to investment grade (A3) and $4.1B of Macquarie preferred equity, letting shareholders keep >80% of new sites while reducing reliance on public markets. [Q3 FY2026 call]
Repeatable campus model: once a campus lands an anchor tenant, expanding it (more buildings, more tenants) is easier than starting new sites — a path to 5-6 GW over time. [Q3 FY2026 call]

financial_performance.analyst_view: Financially, Applied Digital is exactly what an early-stage infrastructure developer looks like: big revenue growth (+139%), positive adjusted EBITDA, but sizeable GAAP losses, heavy CapEx, and lots of debt/financing engineering. The bull case is concrete and improving — a $16B backlog, a 100 MW building cash-flowing, a CoreWeave SPV upgraded to investment grade, and a clear ramp as buildings energize. The bear case is execution and balance-sheet risk: it must build ~900 MW on time/on budget, keep financing it, and refinance cheaply, all while losing money.

final_research_summary.one_paragraph: Applied Digital (APLD) is NOT a chipmaker — it is a developer, owner, and operator of large-scale AI/HPC data centers (the physical 'AI factories' of power, buildings, and liquid cooling), which it leases to AI compute providers under long-term (15-30 year) contracts. It is essentially an AI-infrastructure landlord in a heavy CONSTRUCTION phase, so it is currently loss-making and a normal P/E is meaningless — the right lens is contracted backlog, NOI, EBITDA, tenant credit, and cost of capital. Fiscal Q3 2026 (quarter ended 2026-02-28) showed the model turning on: revenue $126.6M (+139% YoY) and adjusted EBITDA $44.1M as its first 100 MW building (leased to neocloud CoreWeave) cash-flowed, even as a GAAP net loss of $100.9M reflected a non-cash Cloud write-down and heavy stock comp. The big picture is a ~$16B contracted lease backlog (~$11B CoreWeave + ~$5.5B an investment-grade hyperscaler), ~900 MW under construction (one-tenth energized), four more sites (~1 GW) being marketed, and a path management lays out toward 5-6 GW and $1B+ of high-margin NOI within five years. Two developments de-risk the story: the CoreWeave lease SPV was upgraded from BB to investment-grade A3 (lowering financing costs), and Applied Digital has $4.1B of Macquarie preferred equity to fund new sites while keeping >80% ownership. It is also spinning off its GPU-Cloud unit (ChronoScale) and backing an independent power producer (Base Electron). The balance sheet is solid for the stage ($2.1B cash, $2.7B debt, no big maturities for two years). Valuation is entirely forward-looking: ~$12.2B market cap / ~$12.8B enterprise value (the stock is up ~5x in a year, with a 52-week range of $9.02-$50.73) for a pre-NOI developer — roughly 13x the $1B five-year NOI target. So what is FACT is real revenue inflection, a large contracted backlog, an improved tenant credit, and a strong balance sheet; what is being PRICED is successful conversion of that backlog into a cheap-financed NOI annuity. Analysts are 'Strong Buy' with an average target ($71) ~66% ABOVE the price. The central debates are execution (build ~900 MW+ on time), financing (refinance cheaply — the 'tipping point'), and CoreWeave concentration — not whether AI data-center demand exists.
